relevant_context:
Archival Description Title: Visual History Archive.
Scope and Content: This important collection contains testimonies of Jewish survivors, rescuers, political prisoners, war crimes trial participants, Roma survivors, … etc. about their life before, during and after the Shoah. It is a crucial source for the history of the Holocaust. On average, the interviews are about 2 hours in length. At the time of writing, the geographical keyword “Belgium” was attributed to 2136 testimonies. 433 Belgian towns, cities and places are mentioned. The interviews provide information on all aspects of Jewish life in Belgium – political, religious, social and cultural life, youth movements, immigration, the living conditions of refugees, pre-war anti-Semitism, integration and assimilation in Belgian society, the outbreak of the Second World War, the first anti-Jewish laws, the Association des Juifs en Belgique, internment in and deportation from the Dossin-barracks in Malines, life in the concentration and death camps, the return to Belgium and reconstruction of the Jewish communities, emigration and aliyah, … Furthermore, there are biographical profiles for every interviewee, available via the online database.
Extent: 51,696 interviews (over 105,000 hours of video) at the time of writing.









Holding Archive: USC Shoah Foundation – Institute for Visual History and Education

Archival Description Title: Personal documentation on Jewish life in Belgium during the Holocaust.
Scope and Content: This fonds contains various documents (in many cases, copies) pertaining to the fate of the Jews in Belgium during the Second World War – including copies of the newspaper Le Flambeau, a list of Jewish children hidden by the Comité de Défense des Juifs, lists of resistance fighters, documents concerning war criminals, … and many other copies documents from archives kept by various organisations and institutions in Belgium.
Extent: ca. 150 files.








History: Some of the documentation in this Record Group was submitted by Serge and Beate Klarsfeld
Holding Archive: ארכיון יד ושם / Yad Vashem Archives

Based on the provided context, here is an overview of the situation of Belgium during the Holocaust:

### **Persecution and Deportation of Jews in Belgium**
1. **Pre-War Context**:
   - The testimonies in the **Visual History Archive** (USC Shoah Foundation) highlight aspects of Jewish life in Belgium before the war, including political, religious, social, and cultural dynamics. Pre-war anti-Semitism and integration/assimilation into Belgian society are documented.
   - The **Association des Juifs en Belgique** (Association of Jews in Belgium) played a role in organizing the Jewish community during this period.

2. **German Occupation and Anti-Jewish Measures**:
   - After Germany invaded Belgium in May 1940, anti-Jewish laws were gradually imposed, mirroring those in Nazi Germany.
   - The **War Crimes Commission in Belgium** prepared a report on the persecution of Jews during the war, detailing the systematic measures taken against them (available in the **Yad Vashem Archives**).

3. **Dossin Barracks (Kazerne Dossin) in Mechelen (Malines)**:
   - The **Dossin Barracks** served as the main transit camp for Belgian Jews and Roma before deportation to Auschwitz-Birkenau and other extermination camps.
   - The **Visual History Archive** includes testimonies on internment in and deportation from Dossin, as well as life in concentration and death camps.

4. **Resistance and Survival**:
   - The **Comité de Défense des Juifs** (Jewish Defense Committee) was active in organizing resistance, hiding children, and documenting war crimes.
   - The **Lavon Institute** holds files on persecutions, pogroms, self-defense, and aid to victims in Belgium, including events organized by Jewish communities in Brussels in 1946.
   - The **Yad Vashem Archives** also contain personal documentation on Jewish life in Belgium during the Holocaust, including lists of hidden children, resistance fighters, and war criminals.

5. **Post-War Reconstruction**:
   - After liberation, survivors returned to Belgium, and Jewish communities began rebuilding. Some emigrated to Israel (**aliyah**) or other countries.
   - The **Visual History Archive** includes testimonies on the return to Belgium and the reconstruction of Jewish life.

### **Key Archival Sources Mentioned**:
- **Visual History Archive (USC Shoah Foundation)**: [Link to testimonies with "Belgium" keyword](http://lod.ehri-project-test.eu/dates/1881-01-01) (2,136 testimonies).

- **Lavon Institute**: Files on Belgium ([Persecutions, pogroms, self-defense](http://lod.ehri-project-test.eu/dates/1881-01-01)).
- **Yad Vashem Archives (Personal Documentation)**: [Fonds on Jewish life in Belgium](http://collections1.yadvashem.org/notebook_ext.asp?site=sapir&item=10611958&lang=ENG&menu=1).
